theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Doctrine of Sin (Hamartiology)
summary: The Fall, original sin, total depravity, the noetic effects of sin, sin’s universality
readingInstruction: Re-read Genesis 3:1-24, yesterday’s passage, and then read Romans 5:12-21. These two passages together form the backbone of the Christian doctrine of sin. Genesis tells the story; Romans tells you what the story means. Read slowly, especially the Romans passage, which is one of the densest in the New Testament.
settingTheScene:
Yesterday you read the Fall in Genesis 3, the narrative of how sin entered the world. Today we step back to ask the larger question: what exactly happened, and what does it mean for every human being who has ever lived? This is the doctrine of sin, sometimes called hamartiology.

The doctrine of sin is the most empirically verifiable doctrine in all of Christianity. You see its effects every day, in yourself and in everyone you know. The problem is not knowing whether something is wrong with humanity. The problem is understanding what is wrong, how deep it goes, and what can be done about it. Genesis 3 and Romans 5 give us the answer. Today we explore what they teach.
observation: Romans 5:12 traces sin and death back to one man: “sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin.” The doctrine of original sin is not invented; it is taught.

Notice the parallel Paul builds: “as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (5:19). Adam and Christ stand opposite each other.
Death is described as reigning “from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam.” Death affects even those who did not personally break a specific command.
The Greek word for “sin” (hamartia) means “missing the mark”, failing to be or do what God made us to be and do.
Genesis 3 shows sin entering through doubt of God’s word, distrust of God’s character, and the desire to define good and evil for oneself.
The first effect of sin is shame and hiding. The image-bearers who walked with God now flee from him.
Sin’s consequences ripple outward: from the relationship with God (alienation), to the marriage relationship (blame), to the body (death), to the ground itself (cursed).
doctrinalFocus:
The Christian doctrine of sin makes four claims that distinguish it from every other diagnosis of the human condition.

First, sin is universal. Every human being, without exception (Christ alone excepted), is a sinner. This is not a claim about culture or upbringing or environment. It is a claim about human nature itself, since the Fall. “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). You did not choose to become a sinner; you were born one. Even before you committed your first conscious act of disobedience, you were already inheriting the corrupted nature passed down from Adam.

Second, sin is deep. The traditional name for this is “total depravity,” and the term is often misunderstood. It does not mean every human is as evil as they could possibly be, clearly people are capable of impressive virtues, kindnesses, and acts of love. What it means is that sin has touched every part of human existence, the mind, the will, the affections, the body, the conscience. There is no part of you that is untainted, no morally neutral zone that sin has not penetrated. This is why Paul says even our good works, apart from Christ, are insufficient. Sin runs all the way down.

Third, sin is inherited. This is the doctrine of original sin. When Adam fell, he did not fall as a private individual but as the federal head of humanity, the representative in whom all his descendants are reckoned. Paul makes this explicit in Romans 5: through Adam, sin and death spread to all. This is why babies die, why every culture in every era produces both wonders and atrocities, why your own heart deceives even you. The corruption did not start with you; it was waiting for you the moment you were conceived.

Fourth, sin is offensive to God. This is what makes sin sin and not merely failure or error. Sin is a moral assault on the holiness of God. It is treason against the rightful Lord of creation. It deserves judgment, not just because God is angry, but because God is just. A holy God cannot be indifferent to sin without ceasing to be holy.

These four claims paint a picture darker than most modern people are comfortable with. But notice what they make possible. If sin is universal, no one can save themselves by being a better person, and so no one is left behind, every human equally needs grace. If sin is deep, surface-level moralism cannot fix us, and so the gospel offers a new heart, not a self-improvement program. If sin is inherited, salvation must also be inherited from a new representative, and that representative is Christ, the second Adam. If sin is offensive to God, it must be punished, and Christ has taken that punishment on himself.

The doctrine of sin is bad news. But every Christian doctrine of grace is only good news because of how bad the news of sin is. The depth of the disease tells you the depth of the cure. If sin were only a failure of effort, Christ’s death on the cross would be absurd overkill. But if sin is what Scripture says it is, then Christ’s death is precisely what we need.
interpretation:
Genesis 3 and Romans 5 together tell us not just what sin is, but how it works.

In Genesis 3, sin begins with doubting God’s word. The serpent’s first question is “Did God actually say?” Before Eve had eaten anything, the soil of her heart was being prepared for rebellion by being asked to question what God had spoken. This is still how sin operates today. Long before a Christian falls into open disobedience, the foundation has usually been laid by questioning whether God really said what he said, really means what he means, really cares what he cares about. Watch the pattern. Sin always starts with the word.

Then sin moves to distrust of God’s character. The serpent does not just question the content of God’s word; he attacks God’s motives. “God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God.” Translated: God is holding out on you. He is not generous; he is stingy. He is not a good Father; he is a withholding tyrant. This lie is in every temptation you face. If you could see that God is good and that his command is for your flourishing, sin would lose almost all of its power. But the serpent works to make God look smaller, meaner, and less trustworthy than he is.

Finally, sin culminates in self-deification, the desire to be the one who decides what is good and what is evil. This is the heart of sin. Not just disobedience to a command, but the assertion of moral autonomy: I will define right and wrong for myself. Every sin is, in some sense, a small repetition of this. Whenever you choose to override what God has said because you have decided your way is wiser, kinder, more loving, or more reasonable, you are echoing Eden.

Romans 5 then takes this story and tells you why it matters for you. Paul’s argument is breathtaking in its scope. The world we live in, full of death, decay, injustice, futility, is the world that Adam’s sin has brought about. Not because each of us has personally sinned the way Adam did (though we have), but because we are all in Adam. The technical term is “federal headship.” Adam represented humanity. His fall was our fall. His exile was our exile. His death is our death.

But that is not the end of Paul’s argument. He sets up the contrast precisely so he can flip it. If one man’s disobedience could plunge all of humanity into sin and death, then one man’s obedience can lift all who are in him out of sin and death. That second man is Christ. Just as we were in Adam by birth, we are in Christ by faith. Just as Adam’s failure was counted as ours, Christ’s success is counted as ours. Just as we inherited death from Adam, we inherit life from Christ. The whole gospel hinges on this parallel.

So the doctrine of sin is not Christianity’s primary message. It is the dark background against which the bright news of Christ stands out. You cannot understand the gospel without it. You cannot rejoice in the cross until you have grieved over Eden. But once you have done both, you will see the wonder of what Christ has done with a clarity that no shallower doctrine could ever produce.
connection: Genesis 1 and 2 showed us what we were meant to be, image-bearers in covenant with God, called to rule the world he made. Genesis 3 showed us what we became, exiles, hiding, ashamed, dying. The doctrine of sin is the bridge that explains every other tension in Scripture. It is why the law has to be given. It is why blood has to be shed. It is why prophets weep and kings fail. It is why God’s people need a Savior, not just a teacher or a king. And it is why, when Christ enters the world in the New Testament, he comes not as a moral example to imitate but as a substitute to die. As you continue reading, you will see this doctrine confirmed at every turn, and you will see, with growing clarity, why the gospel of Christ is the only answer to the catastrophe of Genesis 3.
application:
Take sin seriously. This is hard in a culture that wants to soften every category and rename every failure. But you will not grow as a Christian if you minimize what is actually wrong with you. The depth of grace can only be felt by those who have honestly faced the depth of sin.

Practically, three habits help. First, regular self-examination, not in a morbid way, but honestly asking God to show you where you have sinned in the past day, week, month. The psalmist’s prayer is a good one: “Search me, O God, and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23). Second, confession, both in personal prayer and, when appropriate, with trusted believers. Sin loses much of its power when it is brought into the light. Third, repentance, not just feeling bad about sin, but turning from it toward Christ, again and again.

But also, take grace seriously. The doctrine of sin is not meant to keep you in despair. It is meant to drive you to Christ. If you are in him, the verdict over you is no longer “in Adam, condemned” but “in Christ, justified.” The sin still in you does not define you; Christ does. The doctrine of sin should produce humility, not self-loathing. It should produce vigilance, not paranoia. It should produce gratitude, because you know what you have been rescued from.

If you have never trusted in Christ as the Savior who bore your sin and gave you his righteousness, today is a good day to do so. The serpent’s lie was that God is not good. Christ’s death is the answer: God is so good that he sent his own Son to bear what we deserved.
prayerPrompts: Tell God honestly what you see when you look at your own heart, and ask for his mercy.
Thank Jesus for doing what Adam failed to do.
Ask him to keep you close to the cross, taking sin seriously and grace more seriously still.
